vulnerabilities.name: AWS Access Key ID
vulnerabilities.description:
An AWS Access Key ID was detected. AWS Access Key IDs come in different types: long-term IAM user access keys
(starting with AKIA), temporary STS credentials (starting with ASIA), or AWS STS service bearer tokens. These
credentials are paired with Secret Access Keys to authenticate programmatic requests to AWS services. A
malicious actor with access to both the Access Key ID and its associated Secret Access Key can access AWS
resources with the permissions granted to that credential, potentially leading to data breaches, resource
manipulation, or unauthorized charges.

For general guidance on handling security incidents with regards to leaked keys, please see the GitLab
documentation on
[Credential exposure to the internet](https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/security/responding_to_security_incidents.html#credential-exposure-to-public-internet).

- **For Long-term IAM Access Keys (AKIA/A3T prefix)**:

To delete a long-term IAM access key:

1. Log in to the AWS Management Console at <https://console.aws.amazon.com>
2. Navigate to the IAM service by searching for "IAM" in the search bar or accessing it directly at
   <https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam>
3. In the left navigation pane, select "Users" and locate the IAM user associated with the compromised key
4. Select the username to view the user details page
5. Navigate to the "Security credentials" tab
6. In the "Access keys" section, find the key that matches the leaked Access Key ID
7. Select "Actions" dropdown next to the key
8. Select "Deactivate" to immediately disable the key, then select "Delete" to permanently remove it
9. Generate a new access key pair if needed by selecting "Create access key"
10. Update all applications, scripts, and systems that were using the compromised credentials with the new key
11. Verify the old key is no longer active by checking the "Access keys" section shows the key as deleted

- **For Temporary STS Credentials (ASIA prefix)**:

Temporary credentials cannot be manually deleted but will expire automatically. To mitigate exposure:

1. Log in to the AWS Management Console at <https://console.aws.amazon.com>
2. Navigate to the IAM service at <https://console.aws.amazon.com/iam>
3. Identify the IAM role or user that generated the temporary credentials by reviewing AWS CloudTrail logs
4. If the credentials were generated via AssumeRole, consider attaching a deny policy to the role to prevent
   further access until credentials expire
5. Review and reduce the session duration policy on the role to minimize exposure window for future sessions
6. Monitor CloudTrail logs for any unauthorized activity during the credential validity period
7. For immediate revocation, you can revoke active sessions by attaching an inline policy to the role with
   a condition that denies access for sessions created before the current time
8. Update the trust policy or role permissions if the compromise indicates a broader security issue

- **For All Access Key Types**:

After remediation:

1. Review AWS CloudTrail logs to identify any unauthorized activity that occurred using the compromised
   credentials at <https://console.aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail>
2. Check for any unauthorized resource creation, modification, or data access
3. Implement AWS CloudWatch alarms to detect unusual API activity patterns
4. Consider enabling Amazon GuardDuty for continuous threat detection
5. Review and update IAM policies to follow the principle of least privilege

For information on how to manage and revoke access keys for AWS, please see their
[official documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_access-keys.html)
and
[STS temporary credentials documentation](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_temp.html).

commit.message:
fixture: give the scanners something real to find

The first pipeline passed with zero findings, which is useless as a fixture:
an empty result cannot distinguish parsed-correctly from parsed-nothing.

Adds a package-lock.json, without which Dependency Scanning creates no job at
all, pinning lodash 4.17.15 and minimist 1.2.0 -- both with known advisories.

Adds code carrying patterns SAST flags: MD5 for hashing, and a shell exec on
unsanitised input. The AWS key is Amazon's own published example value from
their documentation, so Secret Detection has a real pattern to match while no
actual credential is ever committed.
